title: Connected Components & Bipartite Graphs
summary: Two classic traversal applications built on BFS/DFS: partitioning a graph into connected pieces by launching one search per unvisited node, and testing whether it can be legally 2-colored.

slides.markdown:
[graph-traversal-bfs-dfs](graph-traversal-bfs-dfs) covered exploring from one node. This topic is about two problems built directly on that machinery, with no new traversal logic needed: counting how many separate pieces a graph splits into (**connected components**), and testing whether a graph can be colored with exactly two colors so no edge joins two same-colored nodes (**bipartiteness**).

Both reuse BFS/DFS unchanged — the only new idea is the *outer loop* that launches a traversal from every node that hasn't been visited yet, and, for bipartiteness, tracking a color alongside the visited flag.

slides.sectionTitle: Connected components: one traversal per unvisited node
slides.markdown:
A single BFS or DFS only reaches nodes connected to its starting point — if the graph has disconnected pieces, everything outside the starting piece is never touched. Counting components means: iterate over every node, and whenever you find one that isn't visited yet, launch a fresh traversal from it (which will mark every node in that entire piece as visited) and increment a counter.

The total traversal work across all components is still O(V + E) — each node and edge is touched exactly once overall, just split across multiple traversal calls instead of one.

A graph is **bipartite** if its nodes can be split into two groups such that every edge connects a node in one group to a node in the other — no edge ever connects two nodes in the same group. Equivalently: you can color every node with one of two colors so that no edge joins two same-colored nodes.

The algorithm is a traversal with one extra piece of state: when you visit a neighbor, assign it the *opposite* color of the current node. If you ever find a neighbor that's already colored and it matches your current node's color, the graph isn't bipartite — you've found an edge connecting two same-colored nodes.

![A four-cycle 2-colors cleanly while a three-cycle forces a same-colored edge, the signature of a non-bipartite graph](assets/bipartite-vs-not.svg)

The triangle is the smallest possible counterexample: three nodes force a color to repeat after only two alternations, so the third edge always closes a same-colored pair.

assets.alt: A four-cycle 2-colors cleanly while a three-cycle forces a same-colored edge, the signature of a non-bipartite graph

slides.markdown:
A graph is bipartite **if and only if** it has no odd-length cycle. Walking around any cycle, colors must strictly alternate — after an even number of edges you're back to the starting color, but after an odd number, you're forced into the opposite color from where you started, which is a contradiction if that "opposite" position is the same node.

This is why a triangle (3-cycle, odd) can never be 2-colored, while a square (4-cycle, even) always can. It also gives you a second correctness lens for the algorithm: if the coloring ever fails, there's provably an odd cycle somewhere in the graph, and if it succeeds, there provably isn't one — the two are logically equivalent, not just empirically correlated.

| | BFS/DFS components | Union-Find components |
|---|---|---|
| When all edges are known upfront | O(V + E), one pass | O(E · α(V)) ≈ O(E), one pass |
| Edges arriving one at a time (online) | Needs a full re-traversal per query | O(α(V)) per union, no re-traversal needed |
| Answers | "How many components, and which nodes are in which" | "Are these two specific nodes in the same component," incrementally |

Both get the same answer when the whole graph is known upfront — the real distinguishing case is **online** queries, where edges are added over time and you need "are these connected *right now*" answered efficiently after each addition. That's Union-Find's specialty, covered next.

slides.sectionTitle: "Connected" means something different on directed graphs
slides.markdown:
On an **undirected** graph, "connected" is unambiguous: a traversal from any node in a component reaches every other node in it, and that's symmetric — if A reaches B, B reaches A. On a **directed** graph, reachability isn't symmetric, so "connected" splits into two different claims: **strongly connected** (every node can reach every other node, following edge directions) and **weakly connected** (connected if you ignore direction entirely).

A directed graph can have one node that reaches everything (making it look "connected" from that node's perspective) while still failing to be strongly connected, because the reverse paths back don't exist. Calling a directed graph "connected" without specifying which sense you mean is genuinely ambiguous, not just imprecise.

slides.sectionTitle: Forgetting to restart from every unvisited node
slides.markdown:
Checking bipartiteness (or counting components) by running a single traversal from node 0 and stopping there silently gives a wrong answer on any disconnected graph — the pieces not reachable from node 0 never get checked at all, and an unchecked non-bipartite component reports as "bipartite" purely because it was never examined.

The fix is exactly the outer loop from the code slides: iterate every node, and only skip ones already visited. This is easy to forget specifically because a fully-connected test graph will pass without it, hiding the bug until a disconnected input shows up.

slides.sectionTitle: Calling a directed graph "connected" from one node's view
slides.markdown:
A directed graph where one specific node can reach every other node is **not** the same as the graph being (strongly) connected — that's just saying the graph is connected *from that node's perspective*, which says nothing about whether other nodes can reach back to it or to each other.

Concretely: a star graph with all edges pointing outward from a center node reaches everything from the center, but the center is unreachable from any leaf, and leaves can't reach each other at all. Calling this "connected" conflates weak connectivity (or worse, single-source reachability) with the much stronger strongly-connected property — a distinction worth naming explicitly if a directed-graph problem uses the word "connected" at all.
